hints: Compare breaking a $\text{C-Cl}$ bond in chlorobenzene with breaking it in a chloroalkane like chloroethane. Think about what is different about the carbon attached to Cl.
Recall what lone pairs sit on Cl and on O in phenol, and what orbital they occupy relative to the benzene pi system.
Consider what happens when that p-orbital lines up sideways with the ring pi cloud, and how this affects bond order and bond strength.
walkthrough:
Picture what must break**
Think of trying to pull Cl off chlorobenzene or OH off phenol. You would have to break the $\text{C-Cl}$ or $\text{C-O}$ bond directly attached to the ring. In a haloalkane or alcohol this breaks quite easily, but attached to benzene it resists. So something about the ring must be strengthening that bond.

Spot the lone pairs next to the ring**
Look at Cl in $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$ and O in $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$. Both atoms have lone pairs in a p-orbital that sits right next to the delocalised pi system of benzene. The geometry allows sideways overlap, so do not picture the lone pair staying localised on Cl or O.

Let the lone pair join the delocalisation**
That overlap lets the lone pair electrons delocalise into the ring pi cloud. In resonance terms the $\text{C-X}$ bond gains partial double bond character, $\text{C}=\text{Cl}^+$ and $\text{C}=\text{O}^+\text{H}$ type contributions. A partial double bond is shorter and stronger than a single bond, so much more energy is needed to break it, which explains the lack of reactivity.

Final answer: The $\text{C-Cl}$ / $\text{C-O}$ bond in chlorobenzene / phenol is stronger than in a non-aromatic compound.
A p-orbital / lone pair on Cl / O overlaps with the pi-electron cloud of the benzene ring.
The lone pair electrons delocalise into the ring, giving the $\text{C-X}$ bond partial double bond character.

hints: Recall how strongly the $\text{OH}$ group activates the benzene ring and which positions it directs an electrophile to.
With only one $\text{Br}$ entering the ring to give $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{BrOH}$, decide which two distinct ring positions give isomers.
walkthrough:
Use the directing power of OH**
Remember phenol is hugely activated because the O lone pair donates into the ring. $\text{OH}$ is ortho and para directing. So incoming $\text{Br}^+$ from $\text{Br}_2$ will go to positions 2, 6 or 4 relative to $\text{OH}$, not to the meta positions 3 and 5.

Count the unique monobromo isomers**
Positions 2 and 6 are equivalent by symmetry, both ortho, giving 2-bromophenol, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4(\text{OH})(\text{Br})$ with adjacent substituents. Position 4 is unique, opposite the $\text{OH}$, giving 4-bromophenol with substituents para to each other. In an inert solvent with controlled bromine you stop at monobromination, so these are the two $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{BrOH}$ isomers. In aqueous bromine you would get 2,4,6-tribromophenol, but that is not the case here.

Final answer: Product 1: 2-bromophenol, benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ at C1 and $\text{Br}$ ortho to $\text{OH}$ at C2.
Product 2: 4-bromophenol, benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ at C1 and $\text{Br}$ para to $\text{OH}$ at C4.

hints: For step 1, benzene to nitrobenzene, think which two concentrated acids generate the $\text{NO}_2^+$ electrophile and what temperature keeps mononitration.
For step 2, nitrobenzene to phenylamine, recall the classic metal plus concentrated acid reducing mixture heated under reflux.
For step 4, diazonium salt K to phenol, think what simple oxygen containing reagent replaces $\text{N}_2$ when warmed.
walkthrough:
Nitrate benzene under control**
You need to make $\text{NO}_2^+$ in situ. Mix concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$ with concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ which acts as acid and dehydrating agent: $$\text{HNO}_3 + 2\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{NO}_2^+ + 2\text{HSO}_4^- + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+$$ Keep the temperature at 50 to 55 $^{\circ}\text{C}$. Hotter would give dinitration, colder would be too slow.

Reduce nitro to amine**
Nitrobenzene to phenylamine is a 6 electron reduction. The standard laboratory method is tin plus concentrated $\text{HCl}$ with heating, followed by alkali work up to liberate the free amine. $\text{Fe}$ + conc. $\text{HCl}$ with heat is an equivalent alternative. Think of it as supplying $[\text{H}]$.

Hydrolyse the diazonium salt**
Step 3 has already made the diazonium salt K at 5 $^{\circ}\text{C}$. To get phenol you simply warm K with water: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+ + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{N}_2 + \text{H}^+$$ No alkali or extra reagent is needed, just warm aqueous conditions which let $\text{N}_2$, a superb leaving group, escape.

Final answer: step 1: conc. $\text{HNO}_3$ + conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, 50 to 55 $^{\circ}\text{C}$
step 2: $\text{Sn}$ + conc. $\text{HCl}$, heat
step 4: $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, warm / heat

hints: Recall what $\text{NaNO}_2$ / $\text{HCl}$ at 5 $^{\circ}\text{C}$ does to a primary aromatic amine, and what diatomic nitrogen containing group replaces $\text{NH}_2$.
walkthrough:
Recognise diazotisation**
Phenylamine with $\text{NaNO}_2(\text{aq})$ / $\text{HCl}(\text{aq})$ below 10 $^{\circ}\text{C}$, here 5 $^{\circ}\text{C}$, forms a diazonium salt. Draw a benzene ring attached to $\text{N}^{+}\equiv\text{N}$ with $\text{Cl}^{-}$ as counter ion: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 + \text{HNO}_2 + \text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^- + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Keep it cold or it decomposes, and that instability is exactly what you use in step 4 to release $\text{N}_2$.

hints: Think about how $\text{NO}_2^+$ attacks the benzene pi cloud in step 1 and what happens to aromaticity during the reaction.
walkthrough:
Classify the nitration**
In step 1 the electrophile $\text{NO}_2^+$ is attracted to the electron rich benzene pi cloud, forms a positively charged Wheland intermediate, then loses $\text{H}^+$ to restore aromaticity. An electrophile replaces H on the ring, so the mechanism type is electrophilic substitution.

hints: Count how many $[\text{H}]$ are needed to strip two O atoms as $2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and convert $\text{NO}_2$ to $\text{NH}_2$.
walkthrough:
Balance using [H] as the reductant**
Treat $[\text{H}]$ as a hydrogen atom delivering one electron plus one proton. Nitro to amine needs 6 electrons: $\text{N}$ stays attached but O atoms must leave as water. Balance O with water then H: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_2 + 6[\text{H}] \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Check: 6 H on each side in total, 2 O on each side. This is a reduction because H content increases and O content decreases.
